definition: Cartesian genetic programming is a form of genetic programming that uses a graph representation to encode computer programs.
details: It grew from a method of evolving digital circuits developed by Julian F. Miller and Peter Thomson in 1997. The term ‘Cartesian genetic programming’ first appeared in 1999 and was proposed as a general form of genetic programming in 2000. It is called ‘Cartesian’ because it represents a program using a two-dimensional grid of nodes. Miller's keynote explains how CGP works. He edited a book entitled Cartesian Genetic Programming, published in 2011 by Springer. The open source project dCGP implements a differentiable version of CGP developed at the European Space Agency by Dario Izzo, Francesco Biscani and Alessio Mereta able to approach symbolic regression tasks, to find solution to differential equations, find prime integrals of dynamical systems, represent variable topology artificial neural networks and more.

explainer.lead: Cartesian genetic programming evolves computer programs represented as graphs laid out on a two-dimensional grid. It offers a general way to search for programs and grew out of work on evolving digital circuits.

tiers.eli5: Imagine building a machine by connecting blocks on a square grid. The connected blocks describe a computer program, and an evolutionary process tries different designs to find one that does the job. This idea began with efforts to design electronic circuits automatically.
tiers.practitioner: CGP is applied by evolving program graphs arranged on a two-dimensional node grid. The open-source dCGP project implements a differentiable version for symbolic regression, differential equations, prime integrals of dynamical systems, and variable-topology artificial neural networks. Do not assume that every CGP implementation is differentiable: that is a specific feature of dCGP.
tiers.paperLevel: Cartesian genetic programming is genetic programming in which a program is encoded by a graph G = (V, E), with its nodes V arranged on a two-dimensional Cartesian grid. It developed from Julian F. Miller and Peter Thomson's 1997 method for evolving digital circuits; the term appeared in 1999, and CGP was proposed as a general form of genetic programming in 2000. Dario Izzo, Francesco Biscani and Alessio Mereta developed differentiable CGP at the European Space Agency, implemented in dCGP.

explainer.example: Suppose the goal is a digital circuit with a specified input-output behavior. CGP represents a candidate circuit as a graph on its node grid and evolves candidate programs to search for a circuit with the desired behavior; this circuit-design setting is where the approach originated.

explainer.intuition: Instead of writing a program directly, represent each candidate as a graph of nodes on a grid and let genetic programming evolve that representation. The grid gives the method its "Cartesian" name.
howItWorks: Arrange nodes on a two-dimensional grid.
Use a graph of those nodes to encode a candidate computer program.
Evolve candidate program representations with genetic programming.
Use the resulting program for the target task.
explainer.whyItMatters: CGP extends evolutionary program search beyond its digital-circuit origins and was proposed as a general form of genetic programming. Its differentiable version also connects the representation with tasks such as symbolic regression and variable-topology neural networks.
misconceptions: "Cartesian" refers to the two-dimensional grid of nodes, not to a program written as a table of data.
CGP is not limited to digital circuits; it was proposed as a general form of genetic programming in 2000.
CGP and dCGP are not interchangeable names: dCGP implements a differentiable version of CGP.
